content: The distribution or use of a registered pesticide product may be restricted or regulated to prevent harm. The pesticide law or its implementing regulations will outline the specific procedures for such restrictions, including the conditions and limitations that may be imposed by the registration authority. For example, lower registration fees may be applied to low-risk pesticides, while more hazardous products may face usage restrictions. Comparative risk assessments and the substitution principle may also be applied, which excludes high-risk products from registration if effective low-risk alternatives are available for the same purpose. Additionally, the registration of high-risk products may be revised when low-risk alternatives are registered. In some countries, an independent national statutory body is appointed to coordinate pesticide registration. Regardless of the structure, the powers and responsibilities of the registration authority must be clearly defined in the pesticide law. These powers should include the ability to request additional information from applicants or registrants at any time, re-evaluate registrations, and cancel, amend, or suspend registrations as new information becomes available. Such actions may be necessary if the registration was obtained based on false information, if the pesticide has been withdrawn from the market, if registration conditions have been violated, or if re-evaluation determines that the pesticide is no longer effective or poses unacceptable risks to plant, human, or animal health, or the environment. The law may allow exemptions to the prohibition on importing, selling, or using unregistered pesticides in specific cases where such exemptions are justified. For instance, unregistered pesticides may be imported in small quantities for experimental use or scientific research, such as pre-registration testing. Some countries also permit the import of unregistered pesticides to address emergency situations, such as the emergence of new pests for which no registered pesticides are available. These exemptions must be approved by the registration authority, be time-bound, and adhere to strict criteria to prevent misuse. The legislation should establish a clear application procedure for the registration or provisional registration of pesticides. This procedure must specify who is eligible to apply, typically the person or company intending to import or manufacture the pesticide for use in the country. Large-scale users, such as industrial plantations or national agricultural companies, may also apply. The law must indicate the required application form and the minimum data set necessary to initiate the registration process. Registration requirements may differentiate between new registrations and amendments to existing registrations, such as changes in formulation, intended use, or labeling. The pesticide law should specify the criteria for decision-making and the timeframe for obtaining approval, ensuring transparency and clarity for applicants. Mandatory data requirements may include company details, trade name, common name, formulation, proposed use, application methods, withholding periods, chemical properties, toxicological data, efficacy trial reports, residue trial reports, risk assessments, proposed warnings and hazard symbols, packaging details, storage and disposal methods, and first aid instructions. A sample label containing much of this information is typically included in the application. Countries may also require the registration authority to review data from analogous registration processes in other countries, particularly if the pesticide is already registered for similar agricultural and ecological conditions. The law should outline the criteria for reviewing registration applications, focusing on efficacy and risks to health and the environment. These criteria may include the intended use, occupational health hazards, risks to public health (especially for vulnerable groups), risks to animal health, environmental hazards (including effects on non-target species), conditions of use, history of misuse, availability of lower-risk alternatives, product quality, persistence and residues, pest resistance, and proposed packaging and labeling. Consideration may also be given to international agreements and trends, such as the phasing out of Highly Hazardous Pesticides (HHPs) under agreements like the Stockholm Convention. The legislation should specify the possible outcomes of the registration process, including positive decisions (approval), suspension of the application procedure (deferred decision), or negative decisions (denial). A positive decision grants approval for the sale and use of the pesticide, specifying the crops or pests for which it is approved and any additional conditions or risk mitigation measures. Provisional registration may be granted for a limited period, subject to specific conditions and timely submission of required information. Products may also be registered as severely restricted pesticides, with their use limited to specially trained and equipped users under enforceable conditions. Suspension of the registration procedure occurs when relevant information is missing or other requirements are not fully met, delaying the final decision until the necessary information is provided. The criteria for suspending the registration process must be clear to prevent abuse or corruption. Denial of registration prohibits the manufacture, import, distribution, sale, and use of the pesticide in the country. However, applicants may reapply if new information becomes available, such as changes in the product or its intended use. The law may also allow for the outright banning of certain pesticides if they pose unacceptable risks to human health or the environment under all formulations and uses. Banning is a final regulatory action that prohibits all activities and use of the pesticide in the country, precluding any future registration applications. Countries often maintain a list of banned products and active substances. Banning may result from the registration process or new information, such as the listing of a product under international instruments like the Stockholm Convention or the Montreal Protocol. The legislation should specify the procedure for banning and the responsible authority. When registration is granted, the product is assigned a registration number, and a certificate of registration is issued, indicating the validity period and any restrictions or conditions. The approved label, submitted with the application, becomes part of the registration, and no changes can be made to it without the permission of the registration authority. The legislation should also address the legal effect of registration on who can produce or import the pesticide.
